home.title: The three-body problem
home.visualCaption: Figure eight: three equal masses chasing each other along the same curve.
home.problemIntro: It is a simple question to ask: if you know where three masses are and how fast they move, where will they be later? Each one attracts the other two according to Newton's law of gravitation.

two.title: Two bodies: solved
two.text: Newton showed that two attracting bodies trace ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas. A formula predicts their motion forever.

three.title: Three bodies: no general formula
three.text: Each body pulls on the other two and everything changes at once. Poincaré showed there is no simple general solution and discovered chaos: a tiny difference at the start ends in completely different paths.

periodic.title: Orderly exceptions
periodic.text: With very precise starting conditions, some orbits repeat: Lagrange's triangle (1772), the figure eight (1993) and new families found by computer in 2013.

question.title: Can you predict how three bodies move?
question.body: For two bodies that attract each other, one formula is enough. For three there is no general one: a tiny change changes everything. Here you will understand it by experimenting, no physics needed.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon are three bodies. Satellites and probes are planned with these ideas: the James Webb telescope orbits near L2, a balance point studied by Euler and Lagrange.

how.title: How you will learn
how.body: First a one-minute calibration. Then short capsules with experiments and a tutor that runs them with you. Finally, six real orbits.

steps.capsules: Experiment capsule by capsule with the tutor

orbits.title: Six orbits that come back.
orbits.description: With three bodies, almost any start ends in a chaotic dance or with one body thrown out. But with very precise starting conditions, all three return exactly to where they began and repeat the cycle. These are six of those periodic solutions; most are unstable: the slightest nudge breaks them.
orbits.note: These are not hand-drawn curves: trajectories are generated from published initial conditions and numerically validated.
orbits.conceptText: Each body attracts the other two. With very specific initial conditions, their positions and velocities return to the starting point.
orbits.planar: Planar orbit: the 3D camera changes your perspective, not the physics.

learn.title: Gravity starts with two.
learn.description: To understand three bodies you first need to understand how two attract each other. Move the masses, change the distance and predict what will happen before you check.
learn.formulaText: Force F increases with masses m₁ and m₂ and decreases with the square of center-to-center distance r. G is the universal gravitational constant.
learn.force: Initial attractive force on each body
learn.equalMasses: Because they have the same mass, that force changes their motion equally.
learn.body1Lighter: Body 1 has less mass: the same force changes its motion more.
learn.body2Lighter: Body 2 has less mass: the same force changes its motion more.
learn.animationPlaying: The arrows grow as the bodies approach. The force shown is the initial one; simulation time is accelerated.
learn.animationExplanation: Run a one-dimensional simulation of the bodies falling under gravity from rest. It follows Newton's law, and time is accelerated.
learn.animationStaticPending: Calculating the fall for a still view…
learn.animationStatic: Still view of the calculated fall after {time} of simulated time. Animation is off because reduced motion is preferred.
learn.animationDone: After {time} of simulated time, the bodies are very close. The point-mass model stops before the mathematical collision.
learn.animationUnavailable: Animation is unavailable in this view.
learn.scale: Distance to scale; illustrative radii; force arrows on a logarithmic scale. Positions follow Newtonian gravity; the model does not describe real-body collisions.
learn.predictionQuestion: If we double the distance and keep the masses, the force becomes…
learn.correct: Exactly. Doubling r multiplies r² by four, so the force becomes one quarter.
learn.incorrect: The force becomes one quarter: distance is squared, and 2² = 4.
learn.predictionHint: Choose an answer, then check its effect in the laboratory.
learn.rotateHint: Drag the scene to rotate it.
learn.fallback3d: The 3D view is not available on this device. This diagram shows the same experiment.
learn.ratio: {ratio} × the force of the starting setup
learn.noPrediction: You have not predicted anything yet. Choose an answer in the previous capsule first.

numbers.weightRatio: Times the weight exceeds the attraction

pull.title: Any two bodies attract each other
pull.body: Move the masses and the distance. The arrows show how hard each body pulls on the other: there is never one that pulls and one that is only pulled.
pull.discovery: Two masses always attract each other.
pull.more: There are only two bodies on purpose: that isolates this interaction. Later we add a third one and you will see what changes.

mutual.title: Same force, different motion
mutual.body: Release the bodies. The force is the same on both, but the lighter one moves more: with less mass, the same force changes its motion more.
mutual.discovery: Equal forces; the lighter body accelerates more.
mutual.more: Acceleration tells how much the motion changes. For each body it is the force divided by its mass.

numbers.title: Why don't you feel another person pulling on you?
numbers.body: Between everyday objects the attraction is tiny compared with their weight. Gravity is only noticeable when one of the masses is huge, like the Earth.
numbers.discovery: Between everyday objects gravity is tiny.

mass.title: Double the mass, double the force
mass.body: Double the first mass and compare the new force with the starting one. Every extra kilogram pulls a little more.

predict.title: What if you move them twice as far apart?
predict.body: Before trying it, choose what you think will happen to the force. There is no grade: being wrong here is part of the experiment.
predict.discovery: First you predict, then you measure.

check.title: Check it
check.body: Double the distance and compare the force with the starting one. Does it match your prediction?

formula.title: It all fits in one law
formula.body: What you have discovered fits in one line: the force grows with both masses and drops with the square of the distance.
formula.more: The force has the same size on both bodies and opposite directions. If the masses differ, the lighter one accelerates more.

third.title: Add a third body
third.body: Each pair attracts with the same law. With three, each body pulls on the other two at once and there is no formula any more: it has to be computed step by step. Press play.
third.discovery: With three bodies, motion is computed step by step.
third.more: Exact Newtonian physics with point masses and G = 1, no force softening. Normalized units.

chaos.title: A 1% change changes everything
chaos.body: Play the Pythagorean system. Then press “Perturb 1%”: the start changes by 1% and translucent spheres follow the original run. A tiny change leads to another ending.
chaos.discovery: Chaos: a tiny change, another ending.
chaos.more: Chaos is not randomness: the rules are exact and deterministic. What fails is our ability to measure the starting point with infinite precision.

unstable.title: Repeating is not being stable
unstable.body: The Lagrange solution is periodic, but after a few turns rounding errors grow and the triangle breaks. The figure-eight, instead, holds.

energy.title: Energy gives the error away
energy.body: With no external forces, total energy is conserved. Its small change measures the numerical error of the calculation, not new physics.

periodic.title: Order within chaos
periodic.body: Some starting conditions are so precise that the motion repeats forever. Thousands are known; here are six of the most famous.

lab.title: Free laboratory
lab.body: Everything at once and no script: choose a starting point, edit masses and velocities and see what happens.

learn.equal: The force has the same size on each body and points in opposite directions. If their masses differ, the lighter one accelerates more.

simulator.perturbHint: Changes the starting point by 1% and starts again: translucent spheres follow the original run so you can compare.
simulator.readHelpText: Total energy should stay constant: if its change is close to 0%, the calculation is reliable. The center of mass does not move because there are no external forces. Closest separation is the distance between the two nearest bodies: the smaller it is, the stronger their attraction.
simulator.editorHint: Changing a value restarts the simulation from the new conditions.
simulator.collision: Two bodies came so close that the force grows without bound: with point masses this is a collision. The simulation stops here; restart or pick another starting point.
simulator.closeEncounter: Two bodies passed so close that the simulation could not resolve their path within one frame. It pauses here instead of guessing; restart or pick another starting point.
simulator.escape: One body has moved far away from the other two: it has probably been ejected. That is the most common ending of the three-body problem.
simulator.model: Exact Newtonian physics with point masses and G = 1, without softening the force. Normalized units.
simulator.fallback: The simulation needs WebGL, which is not available on this device.
simulator.next: Periodic orbits are the exception: conditions so precise that the motion repeats. Explore the six best known.
simulator.comparison: The translucent spheres replay the original starting point. Largest gap right now between a body and its original: {distance}.
simulator.fromGallery: Loaded from the gallery: {name}. Edit a body or perturb it by 1% to see how stable it is.
